newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says error led to Khalistan reference by Gore.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says error led to Khalistan reference by Gore.

text.p: The U.S. State Department said on Tuesday that an "unfortunate error" led to a reference in a letter by Vice President Al Gore to "Khalistan" -- a name not recognised by Washington for India's Punjab region.
Spokesman Nicholas Burns said the United States had apologised to India over the use of the word, employed by Sikh separatists who have been waging a bloody struggle for a homeland in Punjab.
Gore used the name in a reply to a letter from Gurmit Singh Aulakh, self-styled President of the Council of Khalistan, who is based in Washington.

"Dear Dr Aulakh: Thank you for writing to me regarding the ongoing civil conflict in Khalistan. I appreciate hearing your views on this serious situation," began Gore's Feb. 5 letter, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters.

In response to a question, Burns said that "the United States does recognise the Punjab as an integral part of India -- always has and, I believe, always will ... We do not recognise any kind of Republic of Khalistan."

"There was an unfortunate error in the preparation of that letter. And I can tell you that the vice president, obviously, supports American policy, which is that Punjab is part of India," Burns told a news briefing.
Burns said that the United States had "conveyed to the government of India our regret that this letter was sent. We said that the wording, of course, does not represent our policy.
"The vice president is very well aware of that. And I think this is a closed matter which we'll put behind us with the Indian government," the U.S. spokesman added.
The embarrassing foreign policy gaffe over Khalistan was disclosed in a week when Gore has been under fire in Washington for soliciting Democratic Party campaign contributions from the White House.
Gore is widely expected to be a presidential contender in the year 2000.
In his letter, which has caused an uproar in India, Gore told Aulakh: "Your views are very important to us as the President and I formulate policies to advance the cause of peace around the world."

Punjab has been torn by nearly two decades of violence, in which nearly 20,000 people are estimated to have died in a Sikh revolt put down by thousands of Indian troops. A Sikh party took power in state elections last month in Punjab.
In a statement, Aulakh said that by acknowledging a "civil conflict in Khalistan," Gore's letter "recognizes the Sikh homeland Punjab as sovereign and independent."

"The Sikh nation appreciates Vice President Gore's letter acknowledging bloody hardships which have befallen Sikhs in Khalistan," Aulakh said. "Indeed, the Vice-President's letter energises the struggle to win freedom for Khalistan."
